passage: Ojas, beta, you're worried because Mihir only grunts at you now? Sit, and listen to your old father. When you were fifteen, you did the same to me. I, Harish, went from hearing about every cricket match to getting "fine" and "nothing." I was hurt, I'll admit it. I sulked for a week, and once I looked through your bag, which I'm not proud of. Your mother stopped me. So I changed. I kept the rules few and clear: home by nine, tell us where. And I was simply there, with tea on the balcony every evening whether you came or not. Most evenings you didn't. Then one day you told me you'd failed chemistry, and I didn't shout. After that you told me more. Not everything. Enough.

qa.q: What rules did Harish keep?
qa.a: Home by nine, and tell us where.

qa.q: How did Harish feel when Ojas started saying only "fine" and "nothing"?
qa.a: Harish felt hurt, sulked for a week and even looked through the bag, which Harish isn't proud of.

qa.q: What choice did Harish make when Ojas admitted failing chemistry, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Harish didn't shout, so honesty wasn't punished, and after that Ojas told Harish more.

qa.q: How might Mihir experience a father who stays steady and doesn't shout?
qa.a: Mihir may feel safe enough to come back and share things over time, as Ojas once did.

grounding: A father recalls the hurt of a teenager's withdrawal, and how steady presence, few fair rules and not punishing honesty brought the teenager back.

passage: Manoj worked on a construction site in Dubai, and the only time he could call home was 9:30 at night, Indian time, after his shift. For two years Siddharth had grabbed the phone first and talked about everything. Now, at fourteen, he said "Hi Papa," "Fine," "Nothing," and handed it back to his mother. After those calls Manoj lay on his bunk, staring at the ceiling. He wanted to demand more, or to stop calling so often. He did neither. He called at 9:30 every night, even for one minute. One night Siddharth said quietly, "I skipped tuition to play games at Rohit's." "Okay," Manoj said. "Thanks for telling me. The rule stays: tuition first. But I'm glad you told me." Siddharth talked for four minutes after that. Manoj counted.

qa.q: What time did Manoj call home?
qa.a: At 9:30 at night, Indian time, after his shift.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel lying on his bunk after the short calls?
qa.a: He felt hurt and lonely, tempted either to demand more or to pull back from calling.

qa.q: What turning point came when Siddharth admitted skipping tuition, and why?
qa.a: Manoj thanked him and kept the rule without punishing his honesty, and Siddharth then talked for four minutes.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel when his father thanks him instead of scolding?
qa.a: He'd likely feel relieved and safer being honest, which is why he kept talking.

grounding: A father working far away is hurt by his teenage son's one-word answers and responds with steady calls, a fair rule and no punishment for honesty.

passage: Indu used to know every name in Vaibhav's class. Now, at sixteen, he came home, said "Hmm," and shut his door. At dinner in their Bengaluru flat she asked about school. "Fine." Friends? "Okay." It stung more than she expected. She caught herself about to say, "You never talk to me anymore," and swallowed it. Instead she started a small habit: she left his favourite ragi biscuits on the dining table at nine and sat there with her crossword. No questions. Most nights he took two and walked away. On the tenth night he sat down. "Amma... I got caught copying in the unit test." Her stomach dropped. She breathed. "Okay. What happened?" He told her. She didn't shout. They agreed he would talk to the teacher himself, and the house rules stayed as they were.

qa.q: What did Indu leave on the dining table at nine?
qa.a: His favourite ragi biscuits.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling when Vaibhav answered "Fine" and "Okay"?
qa.a: It stung more than she expected; she felt hurt and shut out.

qa.q: Why did Indu's response to the copying confession matter?
qa.a: She stayed calm, listened and kept the rules the same instead of punishing his honesty, so he'd keep coming to her.

qa.q: What might the biscuits and crossword have meant to Vaibhav?
qa.a: A quiet sign that his mother was there without pressure, which made it possible for him to sit down when he was ready.

grounding: A mother hurt by her teenage son's short answers responds with quiet availability and fair rules, and does not punish him for being honest.

passage:
"How was school?"
"Fine."
"And the science test?"
"Okay."
Pallavi put down the knife. A year ago Jaya would have told her every name in class before her shoes were off. "Jaya, I'm not going to chase you. But I'm in the kitchen every evening, and I'm a good listener."
"Mm."
Twenty minutes later Jaya came back and leaned on the fridge. "Ma. If I tell you something, will I get into trouble?"
"For telling me? No."
"I bunked the last period on Tuesday. Went to the park with Megha."
Pallavi breathed out. "Thank you for telling me. The rule stays: you're in class till the bell. But you told me the truth, so there's no punishment for that."
Jaya picked a carrot slice off the board. "Okay." It was their longest conversation in weeks.

qa.q: What did Jaya admit to doing on Tuesday?
qa.a: She bunked the last period and went to the park with Megha.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when she put down the knife after 'Fine' and 'Okay'?
qa.a: She felt hurt, remembering how Jaya used to tell her everything, but she chose calm over chasing.

qa.q: Which choice of Pallavi's encouraged Jaya to be honest?
qa.a: Promising no trouble for telling, then keeping the rule without punishing the honesty, which makes it safe for Jaya to talk again.

qa.q: How might Jaya see her mother after this conversation?
qa.a: Jaya may see her as someone safe to tell hard things to, which could lead to more talks like this one.

grounding: A mother hurt by her teenager's one-word answers stays steadily available, keeps a fair rule and does not punish honesty.

passage:
I'm Joseph, and last year my son Divyansh, fourteen, went from telling me every cricket score to answering in single words. It hurt more than I expected.
At first I clung: I checked his phone and asked ten questions at dinner. He shut down further. Then I went the other way and sulked, stopped asking anything. The house went cold.
What finally worked was boring. Every evening at seven I walked our dog, and I asked if he wanted to come. Mostly he said no. I kept asking. The rules stayed the same: home by eight, phone off at ten.
In March, on a walk, he said, "I've been going to Nikhil's instead of tuition. I don't understand the maths and I was scared to tell you." I didn't shout. We found him a different tutor.
He still grunts sometimes. But he comes on the walks.

qa.q: What time did Joseph walk the dog every evening?
qa.a: At seven.

qa.q: Why was Divyansh scared to tell his father about skipping tuition?
qa.a: He didn't understand the maths and feared his father's anger, so hiding it felt safer.

qa.q: What went wrong with Joseph's first two responses, and what worked instead?
qa.a: Clinging and then sulking both pushed Divyansh away; steady invitations, fair rules and no shouting when he was honest brought him back.

qa.q: What might the daily walks mean to Divyansh?
qa.a: They give him a low-pressure chance to talk when he is ready, with a father who keeps asking without prying.

grounding: A father hurt by his teenage son's distance tries clinging and withdrawing, then finds that steady availability, fair rules and calm at honesty work.
